You actually have an interesting subset of examples, which makes this a difficult answer... but let's take a crack at it:

Places like Netflix and Amazon do it for a fair market.

Imagine owning a grocery store, where you're trying to compete with local grocery stores. Then, one day, Visa and MasterCard threaten to put added "costs" on "non-participating" companies. Now, you have to shell out half a million dollars, to each credit card company, or else the company will charge their customers an extra 50% for each transaction they incur at your stores. Walmart, Kroger, Food Lion, and other chain stores can pay this extortion, but you cannot. It will ultimately lead to you having less customers, who don't want to pay that extra fee to their credit card companies, and the card companies making more money from both the stores as well as the customers.

If laws forcing neutral/fair charges existed (in this hypothetical world), this wouldn't be a problem. These laws could hinder the card companies from extorting their customers and businesses. It could also inhibit them from giving preferential treatment to certain businesses: imagine if Visa created their own grocery store, and offered DEEP discounts for every Visa transaction in these self-created stores, and HUGE penalties for shopping at "non-participating" stores, creating three tiers with you at the bottom.

This is why companies like Netflix are pushing: if your ISP wants you to stream from their service (let's call it Streamie), they'll "tax" Netflix streaming, but make streaming from Streamie free. So, even though you're paying your monthly $9 to Netflix, $100 to your ISP, and should have the freedom to use both, our ISP will throttle Netflix down to 56K modem speeds, and cap your data every month to try to stop you from using Netflix... unless you pay them an additional $100 a month for Netflix service... or, on the other hand, you can use their Streamie service for only an additional $9 a month. With that kind of deal, where Netflix costs you $209 a month, and Streamie at just half of that, which would you choose?

It's not fair, it's not capitalism, and it hurts competition. Businesses don't want to lose business, which means less jobs, and less cash flow. They want a fair playing field, where Comcast won't throttle Netflix, Verizon can't block you from browsing an AT&T site, and AT&T can't force you to buy the HBO package. Without competition, it becomes mass chaos.

Now, ISP's (like AT&T) are pushing for a COMPLETELY different reason. They don't like the current laws, which prohibit favoritism, but they also don't want to have no laws at all... because that sets up room for more laws, just like the current ones, later on down the line. In other words, we have an apple, and decide to throw it away, just to go buy another (similar) apple during the next president's term. They don't want the laws we have now, and they REALLY don't want them 8-10 years from now.

ISP's are pushing for net neutrality, so they can re-write the current laws by "greasing up" the politicians. They want to disguise their favoritism under the moniker of net neutrality. Comcast pays the Senators a few thousand dollars to slip in a little "bandwidth management" (or throttling) when the ISP deems "congestion" is high, and now they can manage their bandwidth back to Streamie instead of Netflix. Take a bunch of members from the House out to a lovely steak dinner, and convince them that allowing users to perouse the internet, without blocking certain sites, promotes terrorism and child pornography, and now they have the ability to block you from browsing the pages of their competitors.

Right now, they're considered a "common carrier," which means they can (in absolutely no way) give any tiering or preferential treatment to the internet you browse... just like your phone and water companies. This was a recent (last couple of years) development, and they were NOT happy about that decision, AT ALL! But, if that was brushed aside for "net neutrality," and "new" laws were written to allow some tiering, or some throttling, or some data capping, then they can start playing their old games.

So, they're supporting "net neutrality," but not net neutrality. They want the moniker of "common carrier" dropped, and regulations put into place... regulations that they "help" write. They want to be able to control what you see and consume, and they want total freedom to do so.

it's not fair, it's not capitalism.

There's no need to think about this hyperbolically. Your telephone (landline that most people don't use anymore), electricity, and other "common carrier" services aren't government run/owned... and there's really no reason/need to say that NN would cause your ISP's to become government run/owned.

These services aren't micro-managed, just prevented from providing favoritism, and I haven't heard anybody complaining that their electric company has become a nationalized private company. Maybe that their bill is too high, but nothing about them being a nationalized private company.

On the contrary, this exact thing happened with Bell Labs (now AT&T), when they became a monopoly: they were the only option around, and they were able to restrict telephone usage to ONLY hardware made by Bell Labs... In essence, even if you were paying for phone service, and bought a brand new/working phone, it wouldn't work on Bell Labs telephone lines if the phone wasn't made by Bell Labs. They FORCED customers to buy their hardware, simply because they could.

This monopoly was squashed, in the 40's, and we now have a TON of telecoms who compete instead of a single, price-gouging monopoly. Growing up, I never heard anybody say that the government should've never messed with Bell... Again, I heard complaints about high bills, but people were happy they could use whatever telephone hardware they wanted. You could use Motorola, Samsung, or whatever you wanted. Imagine a world where you were FORCED to buy an AT&T phone, and that's the only option you had.

And this is a perfect example of what's happening with NN: an ISP doesn't want you using a competitor's video streaming service, so they reduce your bandwidth, to that particular site, to prohibit you from using that competitor's services; Verizon doesn't want you looking at competitors, so they block your access to Sprint web pages; AT&T has an agreement with HBO, so they're going to strong-arm you into buying an HBO package by capping your data and throttling your access to YouTube and Hulu, but allowing unmitigated access to HBO-Go.

The goal of NN isn't to take over, or to nationalize a private company... It's to tell the company that they have a monopoly and they can't use that to strong-arm customers. There are choices, and as customers, we should be free to make those choices.
